questions.q: What is a callback in JavaScript?
options: A special keyword for asynchronous code
A function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later
A built-in object for storing errors
A loop that repeats until a condition is met
questions.explain: A callback is just an ordinary function reference handed to another function, which invokes it once its own work is done.

questions.q: In Node's error-first callback convention, what should the first parameter of the callback represent?
options: The final result of the operation
An error (or null if there wasn't one)
The name of the function that called it
A timestamp
questions.explain: Error-first callbacks reserve the first parameter for an error (null when there's none), with the actual result as the second parameter.

questions.q: Given fs.readFile("wallet.json", "utf8", (err, data) => { ... }), what should code do first inside the callback?
options: Log data immediately
Check whether err is truthy before using data
Call fs.readFile again
Ignore err since it's rarely used
questions.explain: Skipping the err check is a common source of bugs — always verify err is falsy before trusting data.

Deeply nested callbacks caused by chaining dependent asynchronous steps, making code hard to read and maintain
A runtime crash caused by an infinite loop of callbacks
A deprecated JavaScript feature no longer supported
questions.explain: When each asynchronous step depends on the previous one's result, callbacks nest deeper and deeper, hurting readability, error handling, and reuse.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the three problems associated with deeply nested callbacks discussed in this lesson?
options: Increasing rightward indentation with each nested step
Error handling repeated at every level
Difficulty reusing a step locked inside another callback
Callbacks running in a random, non-deterministic order
questions.explain: Callback order isn't random — it follows the event loop's rules covered in the previous lesson. The real pain points are nesting depth, repeated error handling, and poor reusability.
